source: CARDI book "ដំណាំស្រូវនៅកម្ពុជា" (Rice Cultivation in Cambodia), by Men Sarom, Thuy Lina and Pheng Thimuny, published by CARDI, 2007, Chapter 2 (Rice-growing environment), by Preap Visarto, section 2.5 (Nutrients of the rice plant). No elibrary URL visible.
text: This section explains, at a physiological level, where a young rice plant's nutrients come from, in two phases. First (roughly the first 5-6 days after germination), the seedling relies entirely on nutrient reserves stored in the seed itself - the endosperm's starch reserves are broken down by seed enzymes (catalase, amylase, and sucrase) into sugars that fuel the growing embryo before the root system is functional. Root-based nutrient uptake from the external environment begins around day 6 and becomes the plant's main nutrient source from about day 10 onward. Second, once roots are active, nutrients are absorbed from three external sources: nutrients dissolved in soil water, nutrients carried in irrigation/field water, and nitrogen fixed biologically by soil microorganisms and algae (including nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria/blue-green algae in flooded paddy conditions). Key soil-derived nutrients named are nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), calcium (Ca), iron (Fe), silicon (Si), manganese (Mn), and magnesium (Mg), generally absorbed in ionic forms (for example, nitrogen as NH4+ ammonium or as part of larger compounds, and phosphorus as part of P2O5-referenced compounds). Root respiration requires oxygen, which is a particular challenge in flooded paddy conditions where oxygen is limited in the root zone; rice roots cope partly through enzymes (catalase, peroxidase) that help manage the low-oxygen environment, and partly through structural air-conducting tissue that allows atmospheric oxygen to reach the roots through the plant itself.
caveat: This is foundational plant-physiology background rather than a fertilizer application recommendation - it explains why and how the plant takes up nutrients, not what/how much to apply, which is covered by the fertilizer/SSNM entries elsewhere in this knowledge base. Recommend a duplicate-check against those existing entries once repo access is available, though the physiological framing here (seed-reserve phase vs. root-uptake phase) does not obviously overlap with the existing application-focused SSNM content.
